chapter.name: Exploring Forces
chapter.blurb: Two friends cycling through their village feel pushes and pulls everywhere, from the wind against them to something pulling them downhill, launching a chapter on what a force is and what it can do to an object, the difference between contact forces like muscular force and friction and non-contact forces like magnetic and electrostatic force, the special case of gravitational force and weight measured with a spring balance, and why some objects float while others sink in a liquid.

scope_in.item: Force as a push or a pull: Activity 5.1 moving a box by pushing, pulling, lifting (pulling up) and carrying
Force as arising from the interaction between at least two objects; the SI unit of force is the newton (N); an object at rest can still have forces acting on it, balanced against each other
Effects of force: making an object move from rest, changing its speed, changing its direction of motion, changing its shape, or some or all of these together

Contact forces: muscular force (in humans, animals and inside the body, in chewing, digestion and the heartbeat) and friction (definition, direction opposite to motion, depends on the roughness of the surfaces, greater on rough surfaces, also acts in air and liquids)

Non-contact forces: magnetic force (like poles repel, unlike poles attract, a magnet acting without touching) and electrostatic force (charging by rubbing, static charges, like charges repel, unlike charges attract, positive and negative charge)
Gravitational force: the Earth's pull on objects, always an attractive non-contact force, and the resulting vertical motion when an object is thrown up or dropped

Weight and its measurement: weight as the force of the Earth's pull, SI unit newton, using a spring balance and finding its smallest readable division, the difference between mass and weight, and the weight of a 1 kg object on the Earth, the Moon, Mars, Venus and Jupiter
Floating and sinking: buoyant force (upthrust) acting upward on an object placed in a liquid, comparing it with gravitational force to decide floating or sinking, and Archimedes' Principle

concepts.name: Force as a push or a pull
concepts.description: A force is the push or pull that results when at least two objects interact, and its SI unit is the newton.
concepts.idea: A force is a push or a pull applied on an object, and it always arises from the object's interaction with another object.
concepts.rule: Sonali and Ragini's cycle ride shows pushes and pulls everywhere: wind pushing against them, muscles pushing the pedals, and something pulling them downhill. Activity 5.1 shows a box can be pushed, pulled, or lifted (pulled up) and carried; in every case a push or a pull is applied to the box. In science, this push or pull applied on an object is called a force. A force does not belong to a single object on its own: it results from the object's interaction with another object, for example your hand pushing a table. At least two objects must interact for a force to come into play, and when they do, each object feels a force from the other; as soon as the interaction stops, the force on both of them disappears too. The SI unit of force is the newton, written with a small n and symbol N. Even an object that is not moving can have forces acting on it; if it stays at rest, the forces on it are balancing each other, a detail studied further in later grades.
concepts.example: Pushing, pulling, and lifting a cardboard box in different ways are all examples of applying a force to it.

concepts.name: What a force can do to an object
concepts.description: A force applied on an object can make it move, change its speed, change its direction, change its shape, or cause several of these together.
concepts.idea: Force applied on an object may make it move from rest, change its speed, change its direction of motion, or change its shape.
concepts.rule: We apply pushes and pulls all the time without noticing: opening a drawer, stretching a rubber band, a fielder stopping a ball, kicking a football, applying brakes, rolling a chapati, or turning a steering handle. Activity 5.2 asks us to list such actions and their effects, for example a friend pulling a moving bicycle from behind to stop it, hitting a moving ball with a bat to change its direction, or pressing an inflated balloon to change its shape. From such examples we conclude that a force applied on an object may make it move from rest, change its speed if it is already moving, change its direction of motion, bring about a change in its shape, or cause some or all of these effects together. None of these changes happens without a force acting.
concepts.example: Hitting a moving ball with a bat changes the direction of the ball; this is an effect of the push applied by the bat.

concepts.name: Contact forces: muscular force and friction
concepts.description: Muscular force and friction are both contact forces because they need physical contact between the objects involved.
concepts.idea: Contact forces act only when objects physically touch; muscular force and friction are both examples of contact forces.
concepts.rule: Some forces need the objects to be in physical contact, directly through our hands or other body parts, or indirectly through a stick or a rope; these are called contact forces. Muscular force is one such force, caused by the action of muscles when we walk, run, lift, push, jump, or stretch; animals, birds, fish and insects use muscular force for movement, humans have used the muscular force of animals to help with tasks, and inside our own body muscular force helps us chew food, move it through the alimentary canal, and lets the heart pump blood. Friction is the other important contact force: it comes into play when an object moves or tries to move over another surface, and it always acts in a direction opposite to the direction of motion. Friction arises because even surfaces that look smooth have tiny irregularities that lock into each other and oppose sliding; friction is greater on rougher surfaces, and different surfaces make a sliding object stop after travelling different distances. Air, water, and other liquids also exert friction, which is why aeroplanes, ships, boats, and high-speed trains are given special shapes to reduce it.
concepts.example: A ball rolling on a rough playground stops sooner than the same ball rolling on a smooth floor, because friction is greater on the rougher surface.

concepts.name: Non-contact forces: magnetic and electrostatic force
concepts.description: Magnetic force and electrostatic force can both act between objects that are not touching each other.
concepts.idea: Non-contact forces act even without physical contact; magnetic force and electrostatic force are both examples.
concepts.rule: Some forces act even without contact between the objects; these are non-contact forces. A magnet attracts objects made of magnetic materials, and when two magnets are brought close, like poles (North-North or South-South) repel each other while unlike poles (North-South) attract each other; in Activity 5.5, a second ring magnet can be made to float above a first one on a stick because of this magnetic force acting without contact. The force exerted by a magnet on another magnet or on a magnetic material is called magnetic force. Rubbing certain materials together, such as a plastic scale with polythene, or a balloon with a woollen cloth, builds up static electrical charges on their surfaces; a charged object then attracts small uncharged bits, such as pieces of paper, without touching them. Two balloons charged in the same way repel each other, while a charged balloon and the woollen cloth used to charge it attract each other, showing that like charges repel and unlike charges attract; the two kinds of charge are called positive and negative. The force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body is called electrostatic force.
concepts.example: A charged plastic scale, rubbed with polythene, attracts small pieces of paper towards it without touching them; this is electrostatic force.

concepts.name: Gravitational force and weight
concepts.description: The Earth pulls every object towards itself with a gravitational force, and the strength of this pull on an object is its weight, measured with a spring balance.
concepts.idea: Gravitational force is the Earth's attractive, non-contact pull on objects, and weight is the force of this pull, measured in newtons and different from mass.
concepts.rule: Every object thrown up, in any direction, eventually falls back towards the Earth; the force with which the Earth attracts objects towards itself is called the gravitational force, or simply gravity. It acts without contact, so it is a non-contact force, and unlike magnetic or electrostatic force it is always attractive, never repulsive. An object dropped from a height falls straight down, and an object thrown straight up slows down, stops for a moment, and then falls straight back down; this is vertical motion under gravity. The force with which the Earth pulls an object towards itself is called the weight of the object, and since weight is a force, its SI unit is also the newton (N). A spring balance measures weight: hanging an object stretches its spring, and the amount of stretch, read off a scale marked in newtons, gives the weight; on the spring balance in Activity 5.10, the scale reads 0 to 10 N, with 5 equal divisions between each 1 N mark, so the smallest reading it can show is 1 N divided by 5, or 0.2 N. Different objects stretch the spring by different amounts, showing the Earth pulls them with different forces, that is, they have different weights. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in grams or kilograms, and stays the same everywhere; weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, and it changes from place to place. For a 1 kg mass, the weight is about 10 N on Earth, 1.6 N on the Moon, 3.8 N on Mars, 9 N on Venus, and 25.4 N on Jupiter, even though its mass stays 1 kg everywhere.
concepts.example: A spring balance with 5 divisions between each 1 N mark has a smallest reading of 0.2 N; hanging a pencil box on it and reading the scale gives the pencil box's weight in newtons.

concepts.name: Buoyant force: floating and sinking
concepts.description: A liquid pushes up on an object placed in it with a buoyant force, and Archimedes' Principle explains why some objects float and others sink.
concepts.idea: A liquid applies an upward buoyant force on an object placed in it; whether the object floats or sinks depends on how this force compares with the object's weight.
concepts.rule: Pushing an empty, tightly closed bottle down into a bucket of water and releasing it, the bottle bounces back up; this shows that water applies an upward push on the bottle. All liquids apply a similar upward force on objects placed in them, called upthrust or buoyant force. When an object is placed in a liquid, the Earth's gravitational force still pulls it downward, but the liquid's buoyant force pushes it upward; if the gravitational force on the object is greater than the buoyant force, the object sinks, and if the two forces are equal, the object floats. One factor the buoyant force depends on is the density of the liquid. Archimedes discovered that an object fully or partially immersed in a liquid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces, known as Archimedes' Principle: if the weight of the liquid displaced is less than the weight of the object, the object sinks, and if the two weights are equal, the object floats. This is also why a mug feels lighter while it is still under water than after it is lifted out, and why porous pumice rock, full of trapped air pockets, is light enough to float.
concepts.example: An empty, tightly closed bottle pushed under water and released bounces back up to the surface because of the buoyant force the water applies on it.

questions.q: Explain, using Archimedes' Principle, why the same object can float in one liquid but sink in another.
